desc: Ideation and algorithm analysis: identified that top-K pairwise-products restriction is WRONG (counterexample: A=[3,1], B=[4,10], C=[1e9,1], K=2); established correct approach — per-array top-K truncation (valid via downset argument) + best-first search over monotone 3D grid with tree-push rule, O(K log K), no visited set needed.

Implement solve(): fast input via sys.stdin.buffer.read().split(); M=min(N,K); sort A,B,C descending, truncate to M; heapq of (−value, code) with code=(i*M+j)*M+k (0-indexed); start at code 0; loop K times popping and pushing children per rule: (i+1,j,k) if i+1<M; (i,j+1,k) if i==0 and j+1<M; (i,j,k+1) if i==0 and j==0 and k+1<M; print K-th popped value.

Stress-test vs brute force (N≤4, all valid K, arrays with many duplicate values): exhaustive small cases, 3500 random trials, directed edge cases (ties at truncation boundary, all-equal, K=N³, N=1), and the plan-breaking counterexample — all match; dedup verified (each cell pushed at most once, pops nonincreasing).
Verify on samples: sample1 → 31 (hand-traced, matches), sample2 → 30000 (all-equal ties, any K), sample3 → 689589940713840351 (magnitude consistent with formula, < 3·10¹⁸).
Check performance/memory: ~2e6 heap ops with C-backed heapq, heap ≤ ~2K entries of (int,int) tuples (~60-80 MB), runtime ~1-3 s for K=5e5 — acceptable.
